title: What she holds
hook: a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow and flower arrows, and what the hymn says they are
carry: desire and anger rest in her hands
tomorrow: a war told in names, and what she does after the battle

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama began: the goddess born from the fire-altar of consciousness, risen ready for the work of the gods. Today, her hands.
screen: `BORN FROM THE FIRE OF CONSCIOUSNESS.` → `READY FOR THE WORK.`

segments.voice: A rope. A hook for steering an elephant. A bow cut from sugarcane. Arrows tipped with flowers. That's what the goddess Lalita holds in her four hands, in paintings and temple images. An odd inventory: a noose and a goad sound like tools for catching and driving animals, and a sugarcane bow sounds like something out of a children's story. But the Lalita Sahasranama doesn't leave the objects as objects. A short run of names, early in the hymn, says what each one really is.
screen: `A ROPE, A HOOK, A BOW, ARROWS.` → `AN ODD INVENTORY.` → `FOUR NAMES FOR FOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: After the names of her rising from a fire of consciousness, the hymn describes her form, and four names in a row say what she carries. In paraphrase: she holds the noose that is desire. The Sanskrit there is raga: passion, attachment, the pull toward what we want. She shines with the goad that is anger, the hooked stick that keeps an elephant moving or turns it aside. Her bow of sugarcane is the mind. And her arrows are the five subtle elements, the tanmatras, the subtle forms of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, what the senses meet. Desire, anger, the mind, the senses. The Bhagavad Gita traces how dwelling on things breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, and desire breeds anger. These are the hard parts of an inner life, and in this hymn they aren't thrown away or trampled. They're in the goddess's hands. Readers take that more than one way. Some say she holds them, so they have no hold on her. Others hear something gentler: even a person's desire and anger are within her reach. And notice the sweetness: the bow is sugarcane, the arrows are flowers, as in the old stories Kama, the god of love, carries; the path will come back to him tomorrow. Here's the teaching, and you can see it on any shrine: in a Hindu image, what the god holds is a lesson. Lalita's hands say the hard parts of a person aren't outside the divine. They're held, and steered, the way a goad steers an elephant instead of killing it.
screen: `THE NOOSE IS DESIRE.` · `THE GOAD IS ANGER.` · `THE BOW IS THE MIND, THE ARROWS THE SENSES.` · `WHAT A GOD HOLDS IS A LESSON.` · then, large: `HELD, AND STEERED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small want you're carrying today and notice it the way you'd notice a rope in someone's hand: there, held; then one irritation, then the busy mind, then one sound or touch, each seen the same way. Nothing to fix. If you pray, you can offer each to the goddess in your own words; if you don't, let them rest in open hands.
The Lalita Sahasranama. The hymn of names for the goddess Lalita, and today four of them: the noose, the goad, the bow and the arrows.
Your line: desire and anger rest in her hands. Held, not thrown away. Back tomorrow, same hill.

notes: Names paraphrased: 4 cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā (born from the fire-pit of consciousness), 7 caturbāhusamanvitā (four-armed), 8 rāgasvarūpapāśāḍhyā (holding the noose whose form is desire), 9 krodhākārāṅkuśojjvalā (shining with the goad whose form is anger), 10 manorūpekṣukodaṇḍā (whose sugarcane bow is the mind), 11 pañcatanmātrasāyakā (whose arrows are the five tanmātras). Confirm numbering and glosses.
Glossing the tanmātras as 'the subtle forms of sound, touch, form, taste and smell' is a simplification; confirm.

The three readings (she holds them so they don't hold her; a person's passions are within her reach; the sweetness of the bow) are attributed to commentators and 'some readers' without naming a commentary. Kama's sugarcane bow and flower arrows: standard iconography; tomorrow's story (Kama burned and revived) picks this up.
